extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters/court reporters covering trials and court beats
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for reporters who cover court proceedings for newspapers: how to prepare, behave in court, choose what to report, structure court stories, and avoid legal/ethical pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the court system and jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand which courts hear what kinds of cases and how appeals move through the system (e.g., state inferior courts → superior/circuit → state supreme court; federal district courts → circuit court of appeals → U.S. Supreme Court).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that federal courts have original jurisdiction of certain classes (federal government suits, diversity with > $3,000, etc.), exclusive jurisdiction in copyright/patents/admiralty/bankruptcy/federal crimes, and that the Supreme Court will not hear cases purely of state concern unless linked to federal law. This background helps reporters know which bench handles which matters and why certain appeals occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn legal vocabulary and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry and use a one-volume law dictionary and study basic legal language (including Latin terms) so you can think and talk in legal language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read and memorize definitions from past issues' legal terms; obtaining a Latin grammar and reading legal reference material nightly is recommended. Knowing local/legal vocabulary (which varies by region) helps translate civil cases and courtroom language for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate court contacts (clerks and judges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Build relationships with the clerk of courts and judges to get quick, authoritative help and clarifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask clerks hundreds of questions to unravel testimony and transcripts; do not hesitate to consult judges (who may explain rulings in chambers). These contacts speed understanding and provide context unavailable from noting alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest time to become an unofficial lawyer
rubrics_metrics.description: A good courts reporter must invest significant time and energy in understanding law; otherwise they are 'abjectly worthless'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No osmotic process will suffice; become fairly competent in legal reasoning to follow trials intelligently and responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personality-driven or sensational reporting that ignores legal issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute colorful personality detail for accurate explanation of the law and its relevance to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid telling readers 'what they should think' about testimony or focusing on freakish personalities when the legal reasons (e.g., right of way, applicability of ordinances) are what matter to affected readers; such substitution betrays ignorance of law and misinforms the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record attorneys' objections and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Note and report the objections and exceptions lawyers make during trial so you can anticipate lines of appeal and explain their importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a lawyer fails to protest disputed rulings during trial, he has no ground for appeal; by noting filed objections/exceptions a reporter can diagnose an attorney's strategy early and follow the trial intelligently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and understand jury instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to and report the judge's instructions to the jury, as they define the fragments of law the jury must apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury instructions can be dispositive (e.g., whether getaway is part of the murder or a distinct crime); a reporter who ignores instructions misses key context that makes the case comprehensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give civil cases adequate attention and translate jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not neglect civil cases; learn to translate technical civil testimony into readable, interesting copy for the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil matters (property boundaries, estate dispositions, negligence arguments) can be fascinating if explained. Learn local vocabulary and render abstract arguments into human terms to engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contempt of court by following five principal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to avoid conduct or reporting that the judge may regard as contempt: refrain from prejudicial comment, printing stricken material, unauthorized photography, disobeying judicial requests about deletions, and premature reporting of grand jury items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A. Do not comment upon an unfinished case (objective reporting only). B. Do not print material stricken from the record. C. Taking pictures/drawings is subject to the judge's permission—do not defy it. D. Judge's requests to delete or mention lightly are often matters of expediency—consider consequences before ignoring. E. Printing grand jury indictments before formal court report may be contempt; verify timing with court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect judge's rulings about material removed from record
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not publish testimony or statements that a judge has expunged; to mention stricken material is contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you believe the judge abused the power to expunge, discuss with the managing editor before deciding to publish; do not act alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain judge's permission before courtroom photography or drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that taking pictures or making drawings in courthouse premises is within the judge's authority and may be forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A picture taken after a judge's prohibition is contempt. Be mindful reporters increasingly carry cameras and must follow courtroom orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about printing material the judge asked be deleted
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the judge generally cannot prohibit publication of record material (except in limited cases), ignoring a judge's request may invite hostility and lost courtesies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the story is worth antagonizing the judge; sometimes delay or summarize to maintain working relationships. Only very strong stories justify risking judicial hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish grand jury indictments before formal presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid describing grand jury bills or indictments before they have been formally reported to the bench, as doing so may be contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morning-paper reporters face this risk when grand jury finishes late; confirm formal reporting before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid libel; follow legal constraints on defamatory reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of libel risk when reporting courts; libel issues must be handled carefully (see detailed treatment in Chapter 22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the law of libel and ensure you 'have the goods' before making damaging assertions about individuals; consult legal/editional guidance when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid twisting facts—clarify roles and terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure correct identification and roles (complainant vs defendant) and do not guess at meanings of legal terms; ask for clarification when unsure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One inattentive moment can cause major factual errors; when doing cold-court (using clerk records) ask clerks to translate shorthand. Never guess that a mandamus equals an injunction—errors invite public correction and judicial scorn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for two classes of readers: everyday and occasional
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance accuracy for expert daily readers with enticing clarity for occasional readers who will not follow murky prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overvalue faithful readers; ensure the story is enticing and accessible to casual readers while retaining accuracy for specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a tie-back (throwback) in multi-day coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: When cases continue over days, lead later installments with a concise tie-in to previous action, shrinking the tie-in as the trial progresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Day 2 tie-in may be a paragraph describing who, when, and what; Day 7 may be a single sentence; Day 14 may be a short phrase. Keep background long enough to orient new readers but brief for regulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads for court stories can be longer and use a snapper plus summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Court leads need not be the one-paragraph style used elsewhere; use a flash-characterization ('snapper') followed by a summary and allow longer leads when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A courts lead can stretch to half a column; after lead, include verbatim testimony to humanize the story. Choose a one-line snapper (e.g., 'Five motorists paid $215 in fines yesterday.') followed by details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use verbatim testimony judiciously and select representative quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Include short verbatim testimony (a sentence or so) that characterizes or summarizes the case and makes the story human and lively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen closely to choose the one or two statements that best characterize the case. Avoid weak, non-descriptive quotes; prefer testimony that conveys attitude or critical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate testimony form: dialog, Q&A, or summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dialog for brief testimony, Q&A for extended passages in full chronicle, and summary to present much material compactly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing dialog and summary is common; reserve full Q&A for supercomplete chronicles. Use summary when space is limited and select dialog/Q&A when the form adds clarity or color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine appropriate space: routine vs distinctive cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how much space a story merits by distinguishing routine (compact coverage) from distinctive/important cases (more detail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine cases should be reported tightly and clearly. Watch for routine cases that develop unusual aspects (e.g., precedent-setting rulings) which may require expanded coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize multi-case court reports by classification or interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of chronological listing, classify cases (drunk drivers, thefts, etc.) and group the most interesting/important categories first for better structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record each case on a separate sheet, shuffle into a structured piece grouping similar cases; if not classifiable, arrange in order of dwindling interest with best first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle dull trial days by cutting but providing useful background
rubrics_metrics.description: On slow trial days, cut details sharply but include a compact review of previous days to keep readers oriented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hyping expected 'startling developments' that may not occur. A review on the third day of a five-day trial is valuable if written economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use boxed or ruled inserts for small colorful moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Save anecdotal or trifling but human moments for brief sidebars (boxes/ruled inserts) rather than leading the main story with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark such copy 'Box with Superior Court' or 'Ruled Insert with Superior Court' and let the copy desk place it beside the main story; keep these items short and separate from the main focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify cases by the action causing them (concise tie-in sentence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always identify a court case with the action that caused it (e.g., arrest details) using a single sentence if appropriate to orient readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short tie-in reminds readers who may have heard of an earlier arrest what the action was and links installments together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to minimize compositor errors and avoid misleading line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Format copy so that if a compositor misses or merges lines, the printed result won't falsely change the meaning (and risk libel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adjacent lines that, if a line is dropped, could create a false conviction or other damaging statement. Structure and paragraphing can prevent dangerous misprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose lead form with headline and fairness in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide between naming the most interesting case(s) or using a summary lead without names; consider whether a 'name head' is justified and the ethical implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary leads emphasize court action rather than accused names and are useful when many cases are technical. The reporter should weigh whether the offense warrants prominent naming and a large headline; avoid overly sensational 'name heads' for technical or marginal offenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain narrative sequence between lead and body
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever cases are mentioned in the lead (by name or summary) should be detailed in the same sequence in the story to provide clear structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequencing makes it easier for readers to follow rapidly; do not present details out of the lead order.
